correctness.rationale: Uniform rank-copy integration gives \(H_x=\frac1n\sum_v[L_v(x)^2+L_v(x)D(x)+D(x)^2/3]\), including the zero-weight boundary. Weighted averaging yields exactly \(1/3\); Cai et al. Theorem 3 supplies the minimax upper bound. Exclusion of a strict Condorcet winner forces both rivals into interior support and \(x=(3u-n)/n\), a parity-sensitive rational grid. Condorcet inequalities imply \(H_A\ge(n+6)/(4n)\) for even \(n\) and \(H_A\ge(n+3)/(4n)+9(n-1)/(4n^3)\) for odd \(n\). Both strictly exceed \(1/3\) through \(n=12\). Exact rational evaluation of the thirteen-voter payoffs confirms stability; strict derivative and endpoint inequalities prove uniqueness on the full simplex. The standard-library exact-rational verifier additionally checked payoff identities and exhaustively enumerated anonymous profiles through \(n=13\), corroborating rather than replacing the universal proof. References: Cai et al. (2026), Section 3; RESULT.md, complete derivation.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Cai et al. prove existence, stability, and worst-case metric distortion for all \(k\) and voter counts, which covers feasibility of the thirteen-voter stable lottery but not the absence of smaller exclusions. Their general Appendix A covers qualitative exclusion with eighteen voters; neither a general existence theorem nor a single upper-bound witness implies the first attainable finite \(n\) or uniqueness of that witness. The precise thirteen-voter threshold was separately established analytically.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The game also appears as the independent-with-replacement committee version, a rank-copy quadratic activation minimax, or an equilibrium of a three-draw voter-favorite operator. In all these forms the claimed statement is a minimal voter count for zero weight on a strict Condorcet winner, plus a unique thirteen-voter minimizer; source equivalence of the minimax formulations alone does not supply the sharp count. The original committee-without-replacement model is not equivalent because it has different feasible lotteries and tie semantics.

originality.rationale: The qualitative phenomenon is not new: Cai et al. (2026) Appendix A, specialized to \(m=2,k=2,t=1,r=8/9\), gives an eighteen-voter strict-Condorcet winner excluded by a stable two-lottery. The new exact lower bound (no exclusion through twelve), explicit sharp thirteen-voter example, and uniquely excluding minimizer are sharper than and not implied by that eighteen-voter construction. Charikar et al. (2025) give stable-lottery existence and representation, not finite support thresholds; Cheng et al. (2019/2020) study a different committee-distribution stability notion. Published-index search surfaced \(13\)-voter IRV reinforcement and maximin records with different solution concepts, not covering the stable-two-lottery support claim. All conclusions reflect the inspected primary materials, with residual unindexed priority risk.
residual_risks: Unindexed or unpublished equivalent finite-electorate support analyses, possibly in source appendices not exhaustively inspected.
A future proof of a broader finite-support theorem could subsume the thirteen-voter cutoff.

Alternate meanings of stable lottery (distinct committee draws, deterministic duplicate ties, or modified activation functions) are not covered; comparing them without explicit equivalence would be invalid.

value.rationale: Support of a strict Condorcet winner is a central natural normative property of randomized elections. The first failure size is an exact meaningful boundary for current stable-two-lottery methods in the smallest nontrivial candidate set, and the uniquely excluding witness rules out the failure being a tie-breaking artifact among minimizers. The finite cutoff is not implied by existing asymptotic distortion guarantees or by the already-known eighteen-voter exclusion. The parity- and stationarity-based proof identifies the structural barrier, making this more than a routine example.
